schools.summary: Gill: Elihu turns from the friends to Job by name, entreating in a suppliant manner a diligent hearing; the 'wherefore' looks back to his reproof of the three.
Henry gathers Elihu's arguments: he joins not the friends, disclaims their hypothesis, and would make a solemn business of it — so Job should hear 'all his words, not some only.'
Clarke lays out the whole plan of the speech: Elihu offers himself in God's stead, charges Job, and vindicates providence by dreams, inspirations, afflictions, messengers, and the great atonement.
Ellicott hears a profession of sincerity, Elihu answering Job's longing for an umpire (ch. 9:33; 16:21) as one 'made out of the clay' and disposed to deal favourably.
Gill: the overflow of a man too full to be silent, like bottles of new wine ready to burst, who opens his lips that he may speak and be refreshed.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the 'verumtamen' (cf. ch. 13:4) and the 'behold now' (ch. 13:18): a circumstantial, solemn self-announcement, Elihu addressing Job by name as none before had done, ensuring a word of 'uprightness' (ch. 6:25).
Henry: after long silence Elihu opened his mouth with deliberation and design, no light or hasty thing but a weighed opening.
Gill: not his own integrity as subject but its spring — words proceeding from an upright heart, the real sentiments of his mind, not a double or insincere heart.
Clarke grounds it in the Spirit — 'pure science,' no false position or consequence; Wesley: 'I will not speak passionately or partially, but from a sincere desire to do thee good,' and plainly.
Henry turns it against the friends, who condemned Job to serve a hypothesis they did not credit; and urges plainness and clearness in speaking of the things of God.
Gill: every man made by God, not himself; a proof of the deity of the Spirit, one of the Makers of man named in the plural.
Clarke marks the allusion to Gen. 2:7 (the breath of God, the living soul); Wesley: 'I am thy fellow creature, ready to discourse upon even terms.'
Henry: Elihu is God's workmanship as well as his seniors, made by the same hand for the same end — a credential and a summons to use life to good purpose.

themes: the Spirit of God hath made me

schools.summary: Gill: an offer of full and fair liberty to reply when Elihu has done, asking the same attentive, candid hearing he had begged.
Keil and Delitzsch render the courtroom summons ('set thy words in order... stand up'), leading to the undeniable fact Elihu is about to establish.
Henry: Elihu willing to hear Job's objections — 'those that can speak reason will hear reason.'
Gill: Elihu as advocate for God vindicating his providence, or, reading 'I am as thou art,' a frail mortal creature such as Job wished to dispute with.
Clarke follows Good — 'I am thy fellow; I too was formed by God out of the clay,' the word meaning equal or like; Wesley: 'I will plead in God's name and stead, and am God's creature like thyself.'
Henry: Elihu answers Job's own cry for one to plead with God (cf. ch. 13:21), standing in God's stead yet of the same clay (Gen. 2:7; ch. 10:9).
Gill: Job has nothing to fear from Elihu, a man and not God, no king or prince, without majesty or even age to command awe.
Clarke ties it to Job's plea in ch. 9:34 ('let not his fear terrify me'): being Job's equal, Elihu can impose no fear that would unfit his defence.
Ellicott glosses 'neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee' — 'I will deal gently, and not be harsh.'
Henry draws the rule: 'if we would rightly convince men, it must be by reason, not by terror; by fair argument, not by a heavy hand.'

themes: my terror shall not make thee afraid

schools.summary: Gill: the charge taken not on report but on what Elihu heard himself, unless greatly mistaken, which he thought he was not.
Henry: Elihu an ear-witness of what Job said openly, and so openly to be reproved; yet Job had not said in so many words that he was clean — Elihu may press the words harder than they were meant.
Clarke keeps it honest: what Elihu quotes is in the main Job's own words or their obvious sense (cf. ch. 13:27; 14:16; 31:4).

themes: how far the summary is exact

schools.summary: Gill grants no man is naturally clean, and Job knew it; yet since Elihu affirms the words were spoken, he thinks they truly, if unrecordedly, dropped from Job's lips.

Ellicott flatly denies Job ever used this language (his statements perverted, cf. ch. 16:17; 27:5), and says even Elihu could not enter Job's position — that a man is righteous only as trusting God; Keil and Delitzsch set the outcry against a God who 'findeth occasions' as the thing Elihu answers.

Wesley: Job meant clean not absolutely but of no such transgression as warranted so severe a stroke; thus far Elihu's charge was just, and differed from the friends' — grounded on Job's reflections upon God, not on hypocrisy.

debates.question: Did Job really claim to be 'clean without transgression'?

sides.position: Job nowhere used this language; it is a perversion Elihu was incapable of seeing past
Job's self-justification gave real ground for the charge, which is juster than the friends' accusation of hypocrisy

outliers.note: Holds that even Elihu was incapable of entering fully into Job's position — that a man is righteous only in proportion as he trusts God, and, trusting, is righteous with God's righteousness.

schools.summary: Gill: 'findeth' supposes God sought in order to find, raking up lesser sins and the sins of youth to pick a quarrel — the very misrepresentation Elihu means to correct, for occasions are ready at hand.
Ellicott confirms Elihu reports Job's own earlier words (ch. 13:24; 13:26; 19:11), gathering the scattered accusations that God watched his sin and counted him a foe.
Henry: to say God 'findeth occasions' supposes he seeks them as an enemy seeks a pretext — the fault not in feeling the affliction but in reading divine malice into it.
Gill: the stocks a punishment and reservation for further punishment — Job handled as a criminal guilty of some notorious breach of the law, not merely afflicted.
Clarke and Wesley trace the words to Job's own earlier speech; Wesley glosses 'marketh' — God 'narrowly prys into all my actions, that he may find matter against me.'
Ellicott refers the line to ch. 13:27, where Job first said God set his feet in the stocks and looked narrowly to all his paths — a quotation, not a caricature.
Gill: Elihu denies not that Job is just before God and men, but 'in this' — insisting on his innocence with unbecoming reflections on God — he was not just.
Clarke: Job laid charges he could not justify, proof he is not clear before God; Wesley: God greater not only in power but in justice, wisdom, and goodness, so Job casts off due reverence.
Ellicott candidly asks whether Job had not said the same thing (ch. 9:2), especially as Elihu uses the word for man in his frailty.
Henry marks how much gentler Elihu is than the friends ('in this thou art not just'), and finds in 'God is greater than man' enough to silence all complaint.

outliers.note: Questions Elihu's fairness — Job had himself confessed a man cannot be just with God (ch. 9:2), so the charge convicts Job of what he had already owned.

themes: in this thou art not just

schools.summary: Gill: the creature striving against the Creator, the clay against the potter — folly and sin, for men cannot answer him one of a thousand.

Clarke: useless to contend with God, who is 'too wise to err, too good to be unkind' and owes no account; Wesley: the supreme governor gives no account of his judgments, in whose will all should acquiesce.
Ellicott defends Job — he had not striven against God's justice (which he trusted) but against the darkness round His throne (cf. ch. 23:3); notes the variant 'none can answer any of His words.'
Henry: to complain of God is to implead and impeach him — unreasonable in weak, sinful creatures against infinite wisdom and goodness.

debates.question: Had Job truly striven against God?

sides.position: Yes — to complain of God is to strive against him, impleading and impeaching him
No — Job strove only with the darkness round God's throne, trusting his justice entirely

themes: why dost thou strive against him

schools.summary: Gill: God speaks once in dreams, twice in chastisements, or simply again and again, line upon line, not willing that any should perish.
Wesley reads repeated admonition — a second warning when the first does not awaken; Clarke says the general statement is unfolded in the several methods gathered from the following verses.

Keil and Delitzsch take it to open the first mode, God as witness in man's sleep, the night-vision formed after ch. 4:13; Ellicott lists the two ways dilated on through the chapter, instancing Abimelech (Gen. 20:3) and Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 4:5).
Henry: a token of favour that God speaks at all, and of our enmity that man perceiveth it not — God speaks by conscience, providence, and ministers.

sides.position: repeated admonition — the measure of God's patience, warning over and over
an enumeration of the distinct modes/methods by which God speaks

schools.summary: Gill: God's most usual way then — to a prophet for others, or directly to persons, as to Abimelech and Laban.
Keil and Delitzsch keep 'vision of the night' and 'dream' as two notions, the scene modelled on Eliphaz's night-vision, when the senses are locked and the ear prepared.
Clarke defends both dream and vision against the scoffer: many salutary warnings have come this way (cf. ch. 4:12), and to decry all is as wise as to deny the Bible for the sake of foolish books.
Henry gives the season its fitness: the still night is God's chosen room for dealing personally with men, the senses sealed and the mind free for divine light.

themes: dream and vision of the night
the night a room for God's voice

schools.summary: Gill: the opened ears are the internal ears — God opening the heart or understanding to receive what the vision delivers.

Keil and Delitzsch render a confidential preparing of the ear, God sealing the admonition; Ellicott turns it the other way (cf. ch. 14:17), the sealing of a decreed chastisement against the impenitent.
Clarke heads it secret inspirations — the opening of the understanding, not the dream alone, makes men wise; Wesley: 'sealeth — he imprints those instructions upon their minds.'
Henry: God gives the admonition admission (Isa. 50:5) and lodgment, sealing the instruction as wax takes the seal.

sides.position: the saving instruction/admonition, fastened deep in the heart
the decreed chastisement/sentence, ratified against the man who will not repent

themes: he openeth the ears of men

schools.summary: Gill: 'his purpose' is his wicked work, begun or designed — as Abimelech and Laban were restrained by a dream from the sin they intended.
Ellicott makes it the main point of Elihu's teaching: God's purposes are disciplinary, to keep man from the sin he would else commit — so Job might be righteous yet justly chastened.
Wesley: by glorious representations of his majesty God hides pride, taking man off from self-admiration to a sight of his own weakness.
Henry: to withdraw man from his purpose is to change the temper of his mind; God hides pride by hiding the things that feed it, plucking up the root of bitterness.
Gill reads the pit in a double depth — the grave and the bottomless pit — the warning of conscience standing between a man and both deaths.
Clarke marvels at the outward rescues — how many snatched from an untimely death, the pit, the assassin's sword; Wesley: God does it by gracious admonitions leading to repentance.
Henry: that which turns men from sin saves them from hell (James 5:20); faithful are the wounds and kind the bonds of an awakened conscience.

themes: keep back his soul from the pit

schools.summary: Gill: the 'also' introduces a new way — affliction, painful sickness with a voice in it, felt on the very bed where a man looks for ease.
Clarke heads it the method of affliction (cf. Ps. 119:67) and numbers the bones that may become seats of pain; Wesley: 'the second way whereby God instructs men.'

Keil and Delitzsch weigh whether the once-vigorous frame or 'the unceasing conflict of his limbs' is meant; Ellicott renders 'continual strife in his bones' — rheumatism, gout — the second manner God speaks.
Henry: pain turns a bed of down into thorns — an inward, rooted aching of the bones; the sickbed a pulpit, pain the fruit of sin yet a means of good to the soul.

themes: chastened with pain upon his bed

schools.summary: Gill: through pain the sufferer loses all appetite, loathing even bread, which stands for all common and useful food.
Keil and Delitzsch attend to the poetic form and carry the sense on to v.21 — the flesh vanishing 'from sight' or 'from comeliness' (cf. 1 Sam. 16:12; Isa. 53:2).
Clarke: the expressions point out the general nausea felt in almost every disorder.
Henry turns it to the vanity of the appetite — dainties are deceitful meat (Prov. 23:3), and a man may come to loathe what he doted on (Ps. 107:18).
Gill: the flesh all gone, nothing but skin and bones, through strong pain and the loathing of food, the body quite emaciated.
Clarke names the diseases — atrophy, marasmus, consumption — in which the flesh melts and the bones start out.
Keil and Delitzsch work the Hebrew (Keri/Chethib) from a root meaning to grind or rub away — the very bones ground thin under the file of disease.
Henry: the fat and fair flesh consumed till the bones stick out, yet the soul nourished with the bread of life sickness will not make lean.
Gill: 'soul' stands for the body or the person, given up by physicians and friends at the grave's mouth — Job's own apprehension of himself.
Keil and Delitzsch mark the harder case, distinguished by the LXX: not a warning merely but a deliverance from death, which requires a mediator — not a mere human messenger.
Clarke weighs 'soul' as the immortal spirit and 'the destroyers' (Good's 'Destinies'), preferring the plainer pangs of death; Wesley: 'the pangs of death, here called the destroyers.'
Henry: the man given up for gone, all the symptoms of death upon him, the destroyers ready to seize him (Ps. 116:3).

themes: his soul draweth near the grave

schools.summary: Gregory the Great takes the messenger for Christ himself — the Angel of mighty counsel (Isa. 9:6) who intercedes for us (Rom. 8:26), the great Physician who heals by like and contrary remedies.

Ellicott reads the interpreter, one among a thousand, as a remarkable anticipation of the Advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1; Heb. 7:25) — the Son's mediation and the Spirit's intercession — and 'to declare concerning that man his uprightness,' to plead his cause.
Gill will not have a created angel but a minister of the word, an 'angel' of Christ by office, a faithful evangelical minister scarce and rare, one among a thousand.
Wesley reads a prophet or teacher rightly qualified for so hard a work; Clarke a mediatorial or interpreting angel, 'one from the Chief, Head, or Teacher.'
Henry keeps to a human minister — a man of wisdom who knows the voice of the rod, one of a thousand, as needful in sickness as a good physician.

debates.question: Who is the messenger/interpreter, one among a thousand?

sides.position: Christ himself, or a remarkable anticipation of his advocacy and the Spirit's intercession
a faithful minister of the word, a prophet or teacher sent to read the meaning of the affliction
a mediatorial or interpreting angel

schools.summary: Henry: 'I have found a ransom' is Jesus Christ — purchaser and price, priest and sacrifice — a ransom of God's own finding, in which he glories ('I, even I, am he that hath done it').

Clarke heads it the atonement, the propitiation that gives efficacy to all the means (John 3:16); Wesley hears God: 'I will spare him, for I have found a way of ransoming sinners — the death of my Son.'
Gill: the ransom is Christ, on the foot of whose redemption the Father is gracious to the sick man for his Son's sake.

Keil and Delitzsch place the ransom in a real deliverance procured by the mediator; Ellicott stresses that it is God who finds the ransom, not man's righteousness that saves — words that met Job's longing for the daysman (ch. 9:33).

debates.question: How is 'I have found a ransom' to be read?

sides.position: expressly the atonement of Christ — the blood of the Son of God, purchaser and price
a ransom God himself finds and provides — not man's righteousness — anticipating, within its Old Testament frame, the mediation to come

schools.summary: Gill: a literal recovery, not absolutely but comparatively — the wasted frame grown fat and plump, the withered flesh moist, the pale face ruddy again.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the restored body, the flesh swelling with the freshness of youth as the man returns to his younger days.
Clarke turns it spiritual — flesh fresher than a child's means born a new creature, the days of youth the new birth, a child of God through faith in Christ.
Henry holds both in gospel order: interest him in the ransom and his flesh is renewed, for recovery is a mercy indeed when it flows from remission of sin (Isa. 38:17; Matt. 9:2).

debates.question: Is the renewed flesh a healed body or a regenerate soul?

sides.position: a literal recovery of the sick body to youthful health
a spiritual new birth — born again, a child of God through faith

themes: return to the days of youth

schools.summary: Gill: the frame of the soul after healing — the thanksgiving of the restored man, his affliction sanctified, left more holy and humble.
Clarke: the spirit of prayer the breath of new life, justified by faith, seeing God's face with exultation; Wesley: God deals with him as reconciled through the mediator.

Keil and Delitzsch render the sequence of prayer, favour, and joyful sight, carried into the confession following; Ellicott: a beautiful description of the penitent, rewarded according to a righteousness that is the fruit of faith (Gen. 15:6; Ps. 32:1).
Henry unfolds the recovery of peace — prayer accepted, anger turned away, the face of God seen with joy (Gen. 33:10), the atonement received (Rom. 5:11).
Gill lays out both senses — God looking on men to restore the penitent, or (the reading most adopt) the recovered man looking upon, or singing before, others the confession that follows.
Ellicott prefers 'He looketh upon men, and saith, I have sinned' — the confession of the restored sinner — over 'he shall sing before men.'
Clarke: God shines into fallen men to convince of sin, drawing out the cry 'I have sinned, and perverted the right, and it profited me not' — 'it was not equal to me.'
Henry draws the nature of sin (perverting the right, Acts 13:10; Ps. 125:5) and of true repentance — confessing the fact, the fault, and the folly of sin (Rom. 6:21).

debates.question: Who is the subject of 'he looketh upon men'?

sides.position: God looks upon men and shines into them, drawing out their confession
the restored man looks upon, or sings before, men his own confession

themes: I have sinned and perverted the right
the nature of sin and repentance

schools.summary: Gill: God will keep the man's soul from the pit of the grave, and from the pit of hell or perdition.

Clarke widens it to every returning sinner, delivered from the pit of hell to walk in the light as Christ is in the light; Wesley reads a temporal and an eternal deliverance, the life seeing the light in the fruition of God.
Ellicott presses the variant — the better reading 'He hath redeemed my soul... and my life shall see the light,' part of the restored man's confession continued to v.29.
Henry draws the general rule: whoever humbles himself thus shall not come into condemnation but see the light of the living — 'confess and be pardoned, repent and be saved.'

debates.question: Is v.28 Elihu's third-person statement or the penitent's first-person confession?

sides.position: 'He will deliver his soul' — Elihu's statement of what God does for such a man (AV)
'He hath redeemed my soul... my life shall see the light' — the restored man's own confession

themes: deliver his soul from the pit
his life shall see the light

schools.summary: Gill: a recapitulation — God always at work, by dreams, affliction, and the ministry of the word, and 'twice,' repeating when once will not do.
Clarke renders 'twice three times,' again and again, to bring even the stout-hearted home; Wesley: 'all these ways God uses to convince and save sinners.'
Henry: all providences are God's workings and strivings with man (Eccl. 7:14) — if one affliction fails he tries another, then a mercy, then a messenger to interpret both.
Gill reads the pit as the grave (recovery, as with Hezekiah) and, figuratively, the pit of an unregenerate state from which souls are brought back in conversion.
Keil and Delitzsch render bringing back the soul that it may be enlightened with the light of life; Ellicott calls this the key-note of Elihu's doctrine — education and discipline.

Clarke hears a quotation of Ps. 56:13 ('the light of the living'); Wesley grants the gracious design yet disputes that so much done to save renders the lost inexcusable — 'did God ever design to save them?'

Henry sets 'bring back' beside the earlier 'keep back' — the one preventing sin, the other recovering the fallen — that they may be enlightened with the light of the living, and holds the lost inexcusable.

debates.question: Does the greatness of God's saving work leave those who perish inexcusable?

sides.position: yes — so much was done to save them that the lost are without excuse
no — God never designed or did anything to save the reprobate, so what was never done cannot render them inexcusable

outliers.note: Presses an Arminian rebuttal of Henry's Calvinist comfort: 'How much did God do to save them? Did he ever design to save them? If not, how does that which was never done render them inexcusable?'

themes: bring back his soul from the pit

schools.summary: Gill: consider and weigh well what has been said, and attend to what is yet to be said.
Clarke: 'pay the deepest attention to what I have said, and to what I shall say.'
Keil and Delitzsch carry the appeal forward as one connected movement (vv.31-33), a courteous exchange offering Job the floor.
Henry: Elihu bespeaks Job's acceptance and begs him mark it well, for what is intended for our good challenges our regard.

themes: hold thy peace and I will speak

schools.summary: Gill: if Job has anything to object or any answer to the charge, let him speak.
Clarke: 'answer, speak freely; it is my desire that thou shouldst stand clear of all charges.'
Ellicott: Elihu wishes to justify Job before his friends — that his afflictions are not for past sin but a preservative against future defection, so his case may justly be defended.
Henry marks the temper of a true reprover — Elihu contends for truth, not victory, and would have those he reproves justified.

themes: the reprover who seeks truth not victory

schools.summary: Gill: if Job has no answer, let him attend and listen to what Elihu has yet to lay before him.

Clarke's concluding note records the various readings that let the confession run in the first person, and paraphrases the whole passage of Christ the Messenger interceding and the atonement of v.24 — 'one of the best, deepest, most spiritual chapters' in Job.
Henry: those who would show and learn wisdom must hearken and keep silence — Job, wise and good, may yet be wiser by the means of grace.

outliers.note: Closes with a Christological paraphrase of the whole passage and its textual variants, reading the Messenger, the Father, and the penitent's confession as 'a grand exhibition of the way of salvation revealed to patriarchs and prophets.'

themes: hold thy peace and I will teach thee wisdom
a teachable silence to the end
